title: Atlas Roofing Co., Inc. v. Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission
lead: Two employers challenged workplace-safety penalties because administrative judges, rather than juries, had found the violations.

actors.name: Atlas Roofing
actors.role: Employer assessed $600 for an unsecured roof-opening cover violation.

actors.name: Frank Irey, Jr., Inc.
actors.role: Employer assessed $5,000 for a willful trench-support violation.

actors.name: Secretary of Labor and Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission
actors.role: Federal enforcement official and adjudicatory commission under the 1970 workplace-safety statute.

proceedings: The Third Circuit affirmed Irey’s order and the Fifth Circuit affirmed Atlas’s. The Supreme Court consolidated their petitions and affirmed both judgments on the Seventh Amendment question.
limits: The decision addressed the historical statutory scheme, reserved a scheme without judicial intervention, and excluded wholly private tort, contract, and property disputes. Criminal-jury questions were outside the grant of review.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Congress creates preventive workplace duties
paragraphs: Congress enacted the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 after finding existing state statutory and common-law remedies inadequate to protect workers. Those remedies generally addressed actual injuries and deaths. The new federal law imposed safe-workplace duties and authorized the Government to seek abatement orders and civil penalties even before anyone was injured, while leaving state remedies for actual injury available.

A Labor Department inspection could produce a citation, which an employer had fifteen days to contest. An administrative law judge of the Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission would then hear the case. The Secretary of Labor bore the burden of proving both the violation and the proposed order and penalty’s propriety. The judge could affirm, modify, or vacate them, considering seriousness, business size, good faith, and past violations. Unless a commissioner directed review within thirty days, the judge’s ruling became the Commission’s final order.

A court of appeals could review legal questions but had to accept findings supported by substantial evidence on the whole record. A later district-court collection suit did not reopen liability or the penalty. Thus an employer could be required to pay without a jury ever deciding the underlying facts.

sections.title: Fatal accidents lead to two administrative penalties
paragraphs: Both employers in these cases were cited after 1972 inspections at worksites where employees had died. Frank Irey, Jr., Inc. allegedly failed to shore, slope, or otherwise support a trench in unstable or soft material as a safety standard required. The Secretary proposed $7,500 for a willful violation; the administrative process assessed $5,000. Atlas Roofing allegedly failed to secure roof-opening covers against accidental displacement. Its proposed and assessed penalty was $600 for a serious violation. The administrative judges and Commission sustained the violations and abatement requirements.

Irey sought review in the Third Circuit, which affirmed through a divided panel and then en banc over four dissents. Atlas went to the Fifth Circuit, which also affirmed. Both employers challenged the factual findings and enforcement system’s constitutionality. The Supreme Court granted review only on whether the Seventh Amendment barred this administrative adjudication, leaving their criminal-jury arguments outside the accepted question.

sections.title: The employers argue that changing forums cannot erase a jury right
paragraphs: The employers argued that a Government suit for a money penalty resembled a traditional action at law. Such an action in federal court would require a jury on disputed facts, they contended, and Congress should not be able to remove a constitutional protection merely by selecting an agency instead. Otherwise control over the forum could become control over the right itself.

The Government defended Congress’s authority to create public regulatory duties and assign enforcement to an agency. It also invited a broader ruling that Government penalty litigation did not carry a Seventh Amendment jury right even in court. The Supreme Court declined to decide that historical question because its administrative-forum reasoning resolved the cases.

sections.title: The Court distinguishes public enforcement from ordinary lawsuits
paragraphs: Justice White wrote for all eight participating Justices. When Congress created statutory public rights and the Government enforced them in its sovereign capacity, it could assign initial adjudication and factfinding to an administrative forum incompatible with juries. Tax, customs, immigration, rent-regulation, and National Labor Relations Board proceedings supplied examples of permissible nonjudicial factfinding with monetary consequences. Some precedents had not expressly analyzed the Seventh Amendment, but others had. The principle also reached regulation of interstate and foreign commerce; it was not confined to supposedly indispensable sovereign powers such as taxation and immigration.

Statutory creation alone did not defeat a jury right. Curtis v. Loether, addressing a statutory housing-discrimination damages action, and Pernell v. Southall Realty, addressing a judicial possession action, illustrated the requirement to preserve juries when Congress chose ordinary courts for traditionally legal rights and remedies. What mattered here was the public right’s character and the permissible administrative enforcement forum.

History likewise did not make juries exclusive civil factfinders. Equity, admiralty, and some common-law proceedings used other arrangements. The same factual question might go to a jury in damages litigation and to a judge in specific performance. Equity had developed new remedies when common-law relief was inadequate. Preserving jury trial therefore did not freeze every future regulatory remedy into an ordinary action at law. The Court did not simply classify every monetary penalty as equitable relief.

sections.title: The Court affirms within express constitutional boundaries
paragraphs: The employers’ concern about abolishing jury trial prompted an express limitation: the public-rights holding did not reach wholly private tort, contract, or property disputes. The Court distinguished administrative factfinding about private rights when conducted as an adjunct to an Article III court. It also retained final authority to decide whether a jury was constitutionally required in a legal action before a forum ordinarily using juries. Congress’s choice of forum was not unlimited.

Judicial review existed in the actual workplace-safety scheme. The Court reserved whether Congress could assign public-right adjudication and fines to an agency without judicial intervention at any stage. The employers had not challenged the lack of mandatory Commission review of an administrative judge’s findings. Neither feature became approval of every possible administrative arrangement.

On March 23, 1977 the Court affirmed both appellate judgments, leaving the Commission’s orders and $5,000 and $600 penalties intact. It did not retry the violations or remand. Justice Blackmun did not participate, and there were no separate opinions. The decision concerned Government enforcement of new federal workplace duties, not employees’ private injury-damages claims.
